walks.title: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

section.title: The naming
section.line: The synchronicity essay (CW8 ¶840, 1952) says what Jung has named psychoid and why.

stops.text: The latter represents a psyche that is identical in all individuals.

section.title: The naming
section.line: The synchronicity essay (CW8 ¶840, 1952) says what Jung has named psychoid and why.

stops.text: It cannot be directly perceived or "represented," in contrast to the perceptible psychic phenomena, and on account of its "irrepresentable" nature I have called it "psychoid."

section.title: The three reservations
section.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶368): the three reservations on his use of the word, and Bleuler as its source.

stops.text: If I make use of the term "psychoid" 34 I do so with three reservations: firstly, I use it as an adjective, not as a noun; secondly, no psychic quality in the proper sense of the word is implied, but only a "quasi-psychic" one such as the reflex-processes possess; and thirdly, it is meant to distinguish a category of events from merely vitalistic phenomena on the one hand and from specifically psychic processes on the other.

section.title: The three reservations
section.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶368): the three reservations on his use of the word, and Bleuler as its source.

stops.text: The confusion obviously springs from the organological standpoint, still observable in Bleuler1 which operates with concepts like "cortical soul" and "medullary soul" and has a distinct tendency to derive the corresponding psychic functions from these parts of the brain, although it is always the function that creates its own organ, and maintains or modifies it.

section.title: The three reservations
section.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶368): the three reservations on his use of the word, and Bleuler as its source.

stops.text: The latter term is certainly open to misunderstanding, as either it means what is "below consciousness," or it postulates a "lower" and 3* I can avail myself o£ the word "psychoid" all the more legitimately because, although my use of the term derives from a different field of perception, it nevertheless seeks to delineate roughly the same group of phenomena that Bleuler had in mind.

section.title: The form under the image
section.line: The Spirit Mercurius (CW13 ¶350): the psychoid form underlying an archetypal image.

stops.text: The psychoid form underlying any archetypal image retains its character at all stages of development, though empirically it is capable of endless variations.

section.title: The ultra-violet end
section.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶417): the archetype as such is placed at the ultra-violet end of the psychic spectrum.

stops.text: The archetypal representations (images and ideas) mediated to us by the unconscious should not be confused with the archetype as such. They are very varied structures which all point back to one essentially "irrepresentable" basic form.

section.title: The ultra-violet end
section.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶417): the archetype as such is placed at the ultra-violet end of the psychic spectrum.

stops.text: The latter is characterized by certain formal elements and by certain fundamental meanings, although these can be grasped only approximately.

section.title: The ultra-violet end
section.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶417): the archetype as such is placed at the ultra-violet end of the psychic spectrum.

stops.text: The archetype as such is a psychoid factor that belongs, as it were, to the invisible, ultraviolet end of the psychic spectrum.

section.title: The ultra-violet end
section.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶417): the archetype as such is placed at the ultra-violet end of the psychic spectrum.

stops.text: Since other archetypes give rise to similar doubts, it seems to me probable that the real nature of the archetype is not capable of being made conscious, that it is transcendent, on which account I call it psychoid.

section.title: The physics parallel
section.line: CW8 ¶419–420: the psychic spectrum set beside the physicist's irrepresentable models, and what Jung says follows for psyche and matter.

stops.text: When the existence of two or more irrepresentables is assumed, there is always the possibility—which we tend to overlook—that it may not be a question of two or more factors but of one only.

section.title: The physics parallel
section.line: CW8 ¶419–420: the psychic spectrum set beside the physicist's irrepresentable models, and what Jung says follows for psyche and matter.

stops.text: The identity or non-identity of two irrepresentable quantities is something that cannot be proved.

section.title: The physics parallel
section.line: CW8 ¶419–420: the psychic spectrum set beside the physicist's irrepresentable models, and what Jung says follows for psyche and matter.

stops.text: And just as physics in its psychological aspect can do no more than establish the existence of an observer without being able to assert anything about the nature of that observer, so psychology can only indicate the relation of psyche to matter without being able to make out the least thing about its nature. 4,s Since psyche and matter are contained in one and the same world, and moreover are in continuous contact with one another and ultimately rest on irrepresentable, transcendental factors, it is not only possible but fairly probable, even, that psyche and matter are two different aspects of one and the same thing.

section.title: The physics parallel
section.line: CW8 ¶419–420: the psychic spectrum set beside the physicist's irrepresentable models, and what Jung says follows for psyche and matter.

stops.text: Just as the "psychic infra-red," the biological instinctual psyche, gradually passes over into the physiology of the organism and thus merges with its chemical and physical conditions, so the "psychic ultra-violet," the archetype, describes a field which exhibits none of the peculiarities of the physiological and yet, in the last analysis, can no longer be regarded as psychic, although it manifests itself psychically.

section.title: The physics parallel
section.line: CW8 ¶419–420: the psychic spectrum set beside the physicist's irrepresentable models, and what Jung says follows for psyche and matter.

stops.text: Although there is no form of existence that is not mediated to us psychically and only psychically, it would hardly do to say that everything is merely psychic.

section.title: The physics parallel
section.line: CW8 ¶419–420: the psychic spectrum set beside the physicist's irrepresentable models, and what Jung says follows for psyche and matter.

stops.text: The ultimate nature of both is transcendental, that is, irrepresentable, since the psyche and its contents are the only reality which is given to us without a medium.

section.title: The specific charge
section.line: CW8 ¶841, the paragraph after the naming: what the archetypes are said to be and to do.

stops.text: The archetypes are formal factors responsible for the organization of unconscious psychic processes: they are "patterns of behaviour."

section.title: The specific charge
section.line: CW8 ¶841, the paragraph after the naming: what the archetypes are said to be and to do.

stops.text: At the same time they have a "specific charge" and develop numinous effects which express themselves as affects.

section.title: Not localized in one person
section.line: Flying Saucers: A Modern Myth (CW10 ¶851): how the psychoid archetype is said to behave.

stops.text: The psychoid archetype has a tendency to behave as though it were not localized in one person but were active in the whole environment.

section.title: In Jung's letters to Pauli
section.line: Atom and Archetype, the Pauli–Jung letters: Jung's statements of 1951 and 1953 on the archetype's physical and psychic occurrence.

stops.text: With the merely psychoid (transcendental) nature of the archetype, its purely physical occurrence is by no means precluded.

section.title: In Jung's letters to Pauli
section.line: Atom and Archetype, the Pauli–Jung letters: Jung's statements of 1951 and 1953 on the archetype's physical and psychic occurrence.

stops.text: ESP certainly belongs in this context, for if anything at all can be perceived in this field, it is based on the psychoid archetype, which, as experience has shown, can be express itself both psychically and physically.

section.title: In Jung's letters to Pauli
section.line: Atom and Archetype, the Pauli–Jung letters: Jung's statements of 1951 and 1953 on the archetype's physical and psychic occurrence.

stops.text: The characteristic that is peculiar to the archetype is that it manifests itself not only psychically-subjectively but also physically-objectively; in other words, it is possible that it can be proved to be both a psychic inner occurrence and also a physical external one.

section.title: Whole numbers
section.line: Letter 63 (October 1953): Jung on whole numbers and the psychoid archetype.

stops.text: In addition to this, whole numbers possess that characteristic of the psychoid archetype in classical form—namely, that they are as much inside as outside. Thus, one can never make out whether they have been devised or discovered; as numbers they are inside and as a quantity they are outside.

section.title: Pauli's side
section.line: Pauli's own words: the objection of December 1950, and a letter of December 1953 (66P).

stops.text: In quantum physics, there are not just effects that appear with large numbers instead of with small ones, and not only is the term “meaning” not the right one here (which you have written about at great length) but also the concept of the (psychic or psychoid) archetype cannot be used so lightly in the acausalities of microphysics.

section.title: Pauli's side
section.line: Pauli's own words: the objection of December 1950, and a letter of December 1953 (66P).

stops.text: Now it seems to me here that, compensatorily from the unconscious, the tendency is being developed to bring physics much closer to the roots and sources of life, and that what is happening is ultimately an assimilation of the psychoid archetypes into an extended form of physics.

section.title: The late admission
section.line: CW8 ¶599, a note added in 1948 to 'The Psychological Foundations of Belief in Spirits'.

stops.text: Not only the findings of parapsychology, but my own theoretical reflections, outlined in "On the Nature of the Psyche," have led me to certain postulates which touch on the realm of nuclear physics and the conception of the space-time continuum. This opens up the whole question of the transpsychic reality immediately underlying the psyche.

section.title: The last word
section.line: CW18 ¶1208, a letter to Michael Fordham (1955): the term in its late form.

stops.text: Synchronicity tells us something about the nature of what I call the psychoid factor, i.e., the unconscious archetype (not its conscious representation!).

section.title: The model
section.line: CW9i ¶6 and ¶155, and the Dream Analysis seminar of 12 March 1930: the archetype called a hypothetical and irrepresentable model, empty and purely formal, perfectly indescribable.

stops.text: The archetype as such is a hypothetical and irrepresentable model, something like the "pattern of behaviour" in biology.

section.title: The model
section.line: CW9i ¶6 and ¶155, and the Dream Analysis seminar of 12 March 1930: the archetype called a hypothetical and irrepresentable model, empty and purely formal, perfectly indescribable.

stops.text: The archetype in itself is empty and purely formal, nothing but a tacultas praetormandi) a possibility of representation which is given apriori.

section.title: The model
section.line: CW9i ¶6 and ¶155, and the Dream Analysis seminar of 12 March 1930: the archetype called a hypothetical and irrepresentable model, empty and purely formal, perfectly indescribable.

stops.text: Any archetype is really perfectly indescribable, something perfectly empty, but capable of assimilating a certain kind of material of tremendous variation, yet always pointing to a certain archetypal quality.

section.title: The name
section.line: CW8 ¶275, in Instinct and the Unconscious (1919): Jung names Augustine as the source of the idea of the archetype; the vault records ¶270 of that essay as his first use of the term.

stops.text: from whom I have borrowed the idea of the archetype

section.title: The name
section.line: CW8 ¶275, in Instinct and the Unconscious (1919): Jung names Augustine as the source of the idea of the archetype; the vault records ¶270 of that essay as his first use of the term.

stops.text: down to Malebranche and Bacon, still stands on a Platonic footing in this respect.

section.title: The instinct's side
section.line: CW8 ¶339 (The Structure of the Psyche, 1927), CW8 ¶277 and a passage of CW16: the archetypes set beside the instincts.

stops.text: It is not just a gigantic historical prejudice, so to speak, an a priori historical condition; it is also the source of the instincts, for the archetypes are simply the forms which the instincts assume.

section.title: The instinct's side
section.line: CW8 ¶339 (The Structure of the Psyche, 1927), CW8 ¶277 and a passage of CW16: the archetypes set beside the instincts.

stops.text: The primordial image might suitably be described as the instinct's perception of itself, or as the self-portrait of the instinct, in exactly the same way as consciousness is an inward perception of the objective 8 The actual term "archetype," however, is to be found in Dionysius the Areopagite and in the Corpus Hermeticum.

section.title: The instinct's side
section.line: CW8 ¶339 (The Structure of the Psyche, 1927), CW8 ¶277 and a passage of CW16: the archetypes set beside the instincts.

stops.text: In other words, an instinct is always and inevitably coupled with something like a philosophy of life, however archaic, unclear, and hazy this may be.

section.title: As many as situations
section.line: CW9i ¶99: how many archetypes there are, in Jung's words.

stops.text: as many archetypes as there are typical situations

section.title: The aeon
section.line: Aion (CW9ii, 1951), its foreword and ¶136, and Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶589, 1958): the Pisces aeon, and the spring-point's entry into Aquarius.

stops.text: It is therefore only natural that my reflections should gravitate mainly round the symbol of the Fishes, for the Pisces aeon is the synchronistic concomitant of two thousand years of Christian development.

section.title: The aeon
section.line: Aion (CW9ii, 1951), its foreword and ¶136, and Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶589, 1958): the Pisces aeon, and the spring-point's entry into Aquarius.

stops.text: Christian .tradition from the outset is not only saturated with Persian and Jewish ideas about the beginning and end of time, but is filled with intimations of a kind of enantiodromian reversal of dominants. I mean by this the dilemma of Christ and Antichrist.

section.title: The aeon
section.line: Aion (CW9ii, 1951), its foreword and ¶136, and Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶589, 1958): the Pisces aeon, and the spring-point's entry into Aquarius.

stops.text: spring-point will have moved from its present position 18 degrees into Aquarius, the next aeon, that of the Water Carrier.

section.title: The aeon
section.line: Aion (CW9ii, 1951), its foreword and ¶136, and Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶589, 1958): the Pisces aeon, and the spring-point's entry into Aquarius.

stops.text: We are now nearing that great change which may be expected when the spring-point enters Aquarius.

section.title: Enantiodromia
section.line: CW6 ¶708–709, where Jung defines the term (Psychological Types, Definitions); CW13 ¶294, CW7 ¶111 and CW11 ¶526, where he uses it.

stops.text: it is used to designate the play of opposites in the course of events—the view that everything that exists turns into its opposite.

section.title: Enantiodromia
section.line: CW6 ¶708–709, where Jung defines the term (Psychological Types, Definitions); CW13 ¶294, CW7 ¶111 and CW11 ¶526, where he uses it.

stops.text: I use the term enantiodromia for the emergence of the unconscious opposite in the course of time.

section.title: Enantiodromia
section.line: CW6 ¶708–709, where Jung defines the term (Psychological Types, Definitions); CW13 ¶294, CW7 ¶111 and CW11 ¶526, where he uses it.

stops.text: In accordance with the principle of compensation which runs through the whole of nature,, every psychic development, whether individual or collective, possesses an optimum which, when exceeded, produces an enantiodromia, that is, turns into its opposite.

section.title: Enantiodromia
section.line: CW6 ¶708–709, where Jung defines the term (Psychological Types, Definitions); CW13 ¶294, CW7 ¶111 and CW11 ¶526, where he uses it.

stops.text: Old Heraclitus, who was indeed a very great sage, discovered the most marvellous of all psychological laws: the regulative function of opposites.

section.title: Enantiodromia
section.line: CW6 ¶708–709, where Jung defines the term (Psychological Types, Definitions); CW13 ¶294, CW7 ¶111 and CW11 ¶526, where he uses it.

stops.text: What we observe here is a fundamental law of life—enantiodromia or conversion into the opposite; and it is this that makes possible the reunion of the warring halves of the personality and thereby brings the civil war to an end.

section.title: The quality of the moment
section.line: Jung on time: the quality of a moment (CW15 ¶82, Richard Wilhelm: In Memoriam, 1930), kairos (CW10 ¶398), time and energy (the seminars of 4 December 1929 and 8 June 1932) and the unconscious's space-time continuum (CW9ii ¶45).

stops.text: In other words, whatever is born or done at this particular moment of time has the quality of this moment of time.

section.title: The quality of the moment
section.line: Jung on time: the quality of a moment (CW15 ¶82, Richard Wilhelm: In Memoriam, 1930), kairos (CW10 ¶398), time and energy (the seminars of 4 December 1929 and 8 June 1932) and the unconscious's space-time continuum (CW9ii ¶45).

stops.text: Hauer the Indologist is not to blame for this, nor yet the Edda; it is rather the fault of kairos— the present moment in time—whose name on closer investigation turns out to be Wotan.

section.title: The quality of the moment
section.line: Jung on time: the quality of a moment (CW15 ¶82, Richard Wilhelm: In Memoriam, 1930), kairos (CW10 ¶398), time and energy (the seminars of 4 December 1929 and 8 June 1932) and the unconscious's space-time continuum (CW9ii ¶45).

stops.text: Jung: Time is the essential identity with creative energy. There is a Greek aphorism, "Wherever there is creation, there is time." Chronos was the god of light, creation, and time.

section.title: The quality of the moment
section.line: Jung on time: the quality of a moment (CW15 ¶82, Richard Wilhelm: In Memoriam, 1930), kairos (CW10 ¶398), time and energy (the seminars of 4 December 1929 and 8 June 1932) and the unconscious's space-time continuum (CW9ii ¶45).

stops.text: Fate evolves with time, and it is identical with time.

section.title: The quality of the moment
section.line: Jung on time: the quality of a moment (CW15 ¶82, Richard Wilhelm: In Memoriam, 1930), kairos (CW10 ¶398), time and energy (the seminars of 4 December 1929 and 8 June 1932) and the unconscious's space-time continuum (CW9ii ¶45).

stops.text: Fate and time are absolutely identical, fate being the more human aspect and time the more energic aspect. And time is another aspect of energy, for without time there is no energy, and without energy there is no time. Time is measured energy.

section.title: The quality of the moment
section.line: Jung on time: the quality of a moment (CW15 ¶82, Richard Wilhelm: In Memoriam, 1930), kairos (CW10 ¶398), time and energy (the seminars of 4 December 1929 and 8 June 1932) and the unconscious's space-time continuum (CW9ii ¶45).

stops.text: The image of wholeness then remains in the unconscious, so that on the one hand it shares the archaic nature of the unconscious and on the other finds itself in the psychically relative space-time continuum that is characteristic of the unconscious as such.

section.title: The world clock
section.line: CW12 ¶307 (Psychology and Alchemy, Part II, the Vision of the World Clock) and the Zarathustra seminar's statement on the eternal return (pdf p1375).

stops.text: There is a vertical and a horizontal circle, having a common centre. This is the world clock

section.title: The world clock
section.line: CW12 ¶307 (Psychology and Alchemy, Part II, the Vision of the World Clock) and the Zarathustra seminar's statement on the eternal return (pdf p1375).

stops.text: It is a circle, the eternal return. That is probably the historical origin of the idea of the apokatastasis, but that life is a circle is psychologically an archetypal idea.

section.title: The turn as a system
section.line: Van Eenwyk, Archetypes and Strange Attractors (1997): two sentences from his account of chaos and order; the words are his, not Jung's.

stops.text: Mathematically, this self-or- ganization takes place at a homoclinic point, which designates not only where a dynamic becomes unstable, but where it becomes stable as well.

section.title: The turn as a system
section.line: Van Eenwyk, Archetypes and Strange Attractors (1997): two sentences from his account of chaos and order; the words are his, not Jung's.

stops.text: For order is never pure. Like the yin and the yang, it carries within it the potential to turn into its opposite. The same is true for chaos.

section.title: The deeper layer
section.line: CW9i ¶2 (1934, Eranos; rev. 1954): the definition; ¶88: the collective unconscious distinguished negatively from the personal unconscious.

stops.text: A more or less superficial layer of the unconscious is undoubtedly personal. I call it the personal unconscious. But this personal unconscious rests upon a deeper layer, which does not derive from personal experience and is not a personal acquisition but is inborn. This deeper layer I call the collective unconscious.

section.title: The deeper layer
section.line: CW9i ¶2 (1934, Eranos; rev. 1954): the definition; ¶88: the collective unconscious distinguished negatively from the personal unconscious.

stops.text: The collective unconscious is a part of the psyche which can be negatively distinguished from a personal unconscious by the fact that it does not, like the latter, owe its existence to personal experience

section.title: The concept's birth
section.line: CW3 ¶550 and CW6 ¶842 (Psychological Types, 1921): two earlier statements of a deeper stratum of a collective nature.

stops.text: We must rather suppose that they are something like universally existent constituents of the unconscious psyche, which form, as it were, a deeper stratum of a collective nature, in contradistinction to the personally acquired contents of the more superficial layers, or what one may call the personal unconscious.

section.title: The concept's birth
section.line: CW3 ¶550 and CW6 ¶842 (Psychological Types, 1921): two earlier statements of a deeper stratum of a collective nature.

stops.text: But, in addition to these personal unconscious contents, there are other contents which do not originate in personal acquisitions but in the inherited possibility of psychic functioning in general, i.e., in the inherited structure of the brain.

section.title: Inherited possibilities of ideas
section.line: CW10 ¶14 (the 1918 form, in the vault note's dating) and CW8 ¶99: innate and inherited possibilities of ideas.

stops.text: There are, however, innate possibilities of ideas, a priori conditions for fantasy-production, which are somewhat similar to the Kantian categories.

section.title: Inherited possibilities of ideas
section.line: CW10 ¶14 (the 1918 form, in the vault note's dating) and CW8 ¶99: innate and inherited possibilities of ideas.

stops.text: It is rather a question of inherited possibilities of ideas, “pathways” gradually traced out through the cumulative experience of our ancestors.

section.title: Instinct and its correlates
section.line: CW9i pdf p54 (the section The Concept of the Collective Unconscious) and CW8 ¶280, which names the instincts and their correlates, the archetypes.

stops.text: there exists a second psychic system of a collective, universal, and impersonal nature which is identical in all individuals

section.title: Instinct and its correlates
section.line: CW9i pdf p54 (the section The Concept of the Collective Unconscious) and CW8 ¶280, which names the instincts and their correlates, the archetypes.

stops.text: The collective unconscious consists of the sum of the instincts and their correlates, the archetypes. Just as everybody possesses instincts, so he also possesses a stock of archetypal images.

section.title: Inferred from phenomenology
section.line: CW9ii ¶278: the existence of the collective unconscious inferred only from individual phenomenology; CW8 ¶729: a world-image that counterbalances the conscious picture of the world.

stops.text: This disposition I have called the collective unconscious, the existence of which can be inferred only from individual phenomenology.

section.title: Inferred from phenomenology
section.line: CW9ii ¶278: the existence of the collective unconscious inferred only from individual phenomenology; CW8 ¶729: a world-image that counterbalances the conscious picture of the world.

stops.text: Because the collective unconscious is, in the last analysis, a deposit of world-processes embedded in the structure of the brain and the sympathetic nervous system, it constitutes in its totality a sort of timeless and eternal world-image which counterbalances our conscious, momentary picture of the world. It means nothing less than another world, a mirrorworld if you will.

section.title: The definition
section.line: CW6 ¶694 (Psychological Types, 1921): Jung's definition, set against Adler's restriction of the word to the balancing of inferiority feelings.

stops.text: Whereas Adler restricts his concept of compensation to the balancing of inferiority feelings, I conceive it as functional adjustment in general, an inherent self-regulation of the psychic apparatus.

section.title: The self-regulating psyche
section.line: CW8 ¶159 and ¶132 and CW7 ¶274: the psyche called a self-regulating system like the body, and the unconscious as compensatory or complementary to the conscious.

stops.text: Since the psyche is a self-regulating system, just as the body is, the regulating counteraction will always develop in the unconscious.

section.title: The self-regulating psyche
section.line: CW8 ¶159 and ¶132 and CW7 ¶274: the psyche called a self-regulating system like the body, and the unconscious as compensatory or complementary to the conscious.

stops.text: This lack of parallelism is not just accidental or purposeless, but is due to the fact that the unconscious behaves in a compensatory or complementary manner towards the conscious.

section.title: The self-regulating psyche
section.line: CW8 ¶159 and ¶132 and CW7 ¶274: the psyche called a self-regulating system like the body, and the unconscious as compensatory or complementary to the conscious.

stops.text: conscious and unconscious are not necessarily in opposition to one another, but complement one another to form a totality, which is the self

section.title: The dream's other side
section.line: CW7 ¶170 and CW18 ¶1391: Jung on dreams as compensatory to the conscious attitude.

stops.text: That would not be impossible, for in my experience the vast majority of dreams are compensatory. They always stress the other side in order to maintain the psychic equilibrium.

section.title: The dream's other side
section.line: CW7 ¶170 and CW18 ¶1391: Jung on dreams as compensatory to the conscious attitude.

stops.text: Without such a comparison it is impossible to understand the functional meaning of the dream. f. As a rule the meaning of a dream is compensatory to the conscious attitude, i.e., it adds to the latter what was lacking in it.

section.title: Not opposition
section.line: CW5 ¶98 (Symbols of Transformation) and CW16 ¶12: compensatory set beside mechanical and complementary.

stops.text: Since the relation of the unconscious to the conscious mind is not merely mechanical or complementary, but rather compensatory, taking its cue from the anfractuosities of the conscious attitude, the intelligent character of this unconscious activity can hardly be denied.

section.title: Not opposition
section.line: CW5 ¶98 (Symbols of Transformation) and CW16 ¶12: compensatory set beside mechanical and complementary.

stops.text: The deeper reason for this may lie in the fact that the conscious attitude of the neurotic is unnaturally onesided and must be balanced by complementary or compensatory contents deriving from the unconscious.

section.title: The ordering factor

stops.text: My own personal experience, going back over several decades and garnered from many individuals, and the experience of many other doctors and psychologists, not to mention the statements— terminologically different, but essentially the same—of all the great religions, all confirm the existence of a compensatory ordering factor which is independent of the ego and whose nature transcends consciousness.

section.title: The ordering factor
section.line: CW11 ¶447 and CW3 ¶582: the phrase compensatory ordering factor, said of a factor independent of the ego and of mandala symbols in moments of psychic disorientation.

stops.text: Mandala symbols appear very frequently in moments of psychic disorientation as compensatory ordering factors.

section.title: The counteraction as a system
section.line: Van Eenwyk, Archetypes and Strange Attractors (1997): one sentence on the shadow and compensation; the words are his, not Jung's.

stops.text: Because the shadow compensates consciousness, whenever we think we know what the shadow is, its opposite automatically begins to emerge from the unconscious.

section.line: CW2 ¶166 (1904–05): the definition of the emotionally charged complex; CW18 ¶832: Jung on how the experiments led him to the word.

stops.text: I found then that the experiments were almost regularly disturbed by psychic factors beyond the control of consciousness. I called them complexes.

section.title: The name
section.line: CW6 ¶184 (1921), CW8 ¶131, CW6 ¶828 and CW7 ¶121: Jung's definitions of the name and his comparison with a mathematical function; in the Dream Analysis seminar of 4 June 1930 (pdf p674) he says he did not take the term from higher mathematics.

stops.text: I have called this process in its totality the transcendent function, “function” being here understood not as a basic function but as a complex function made up of other functions, and “transcendent” not as denoting a metaphysical quality but merely the fact that this function facilitates a transition from one attitude to another.

section.title: The name
section.line: CW6 ¶184 (1921), CW8 ¶131, CW6 ¶828 and CW7 ¶121: Jung's definitions of the name and his comparison with a mathematical function; in the Dream Analysis seminar of 4 June 1930 (pdf p674) he says he did not take the term from higher mathematics.

stops.text: It has been named the “transcendent function” because it represents a function based on real and “imaginary,” or rational and irrational, data, thus bridging the yawning gulf between conscious and unconscious.

section.title: The name
section.line: CW6 ¶184 (1921), CW8 ¶131, CW6 ¶828 and CW7 ¶121: Jung's definitions of the name and his comparison with a mathematical function; in the Dream Analysis seminar of 4 June 1930 (pdf p674) he says he did not take the term from higher mathematics.

stops.text: I did not take that term from higher mathematics, I learned only later that the same term was used there, meaning the same thing, namely, the function of rational and irrational data in the functioning together of conscious and unconscious, of the differentiated function with the inferior function.

section.title: The transition
section.line: CW8 ¶145 and CW11 ¶780: why Jung says it is called transcendent, and that it is a process and a method at the same time.

stops.text: It is called "transcendent" because it makes the transition from one attitude to another organically possible, without loss of the unconscious.

section.title: The transition
section.line: CW8 ¶145 and CW11 ¶780: why Jung says it is called transcendent, and that it is a process and a method at the same time.

stops.text: The whole process is called the “transcendent function.” It is a process and a method at the same time.

section.title: The living third
section.line: CW8 ¶189 (a living, third thing), CW7 ¶360 (the secret of alchemy) and the Dream Analysis seminar (pdf p674) on the tortoise.

stops.text: The confrontation of the two positions generates a tension charged with energy and creates a living, third thing—not a logical stillbirth in accordance with the principle tertium 7ion datur but a movement out of the suspension between opposites, a living birth that leads to a new level of being, a new situation.

section.title: The living third
section.line: CW8 ¶189 (a living, third thing), CW7 ¶360 (the secret of alchemy) and the Dream Analysis seminar (pdf p674) on the tortoise.

stops.text: The secret of alchemy was in fact the transcendent function, the transformation of personality through the blending and fusion of the noble with the base components, of the differentiated with the inferior functions, of the conscious with the unconscious.

section.title: The living third
section.line: CW8 ¶189 (a living, third thing), CW7 ¶360 (the secret of alchemy) and the Dream Analysis seminar (pdf p674) on the tortoise.

stops.text: Jung: The characteristics of the tortoise are the characteristics of the transcendent function, the one that unites the pairs of opposites.

section.title: The method
section.line: CW14 ¶257 (Mysterium Coniunctionis) and CW18 ¶1554 (1954, in the vault note's dating): Jung on getting to know the counterposition in the unconscious and on the cooperation of conscious reasoning with the data of the unconscious.

stops.text: This continual process of getting to know the counterposition in the unconscious I have called the “transcendent function,” because the confrontation of conscious (rational) data with those that are unconscious (irrational) necessarily results in a modification of standpoint.

section.title: The method
section.line: CW14 ¶257 (Mysterium Coniunctionis) and CW18 ¶1554 (1954, in the vault note's dating): Jung on getting to know the counterposition in the unconscious and on the cooperation of conscious reasoning with the data of the unconscious.

stops.text: The cooperation of conscious reasoning with the data of the unconscious is called the “transcendent function” (cf. Psychological Types, par. 828).20

section.title: The third as a system
section.line: Van Eenwyk, Archetypes and Strange Attractors (1997): one sentence on chaotic dynamics and a higher order; the words are his, not Jung's.

stops.text: Furthermore, that psychological de- velopment is a function primarily of the resolution of tensions (empha- sizing the ego’s awareness), corresponds with one of the more intriguing hypotheses about chaotic dynamics, that of symmetry-building bifurca- tions, whereby chaotic dynamics actually generate a higher order result coming out than existed going in.
